📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

KFC Spain has kicked off a latest marketing campaign that leans on the recent digital-only Grand Theft Auto VI release. In 2026, gamers have become numb to digital-only releases, piles of early bugs, and multiple layers of DRM. However, as GTA 6 is such a highly anticipated release, folks are still entitled to moan about the physical Blu-ray-style case, which opens to reveal absolutely no physical media at all, just a vacant plastic hub and a redeemable online code. KFC Spain is putting things right, as best as it can, by giving away a free fried chicken disc to those bringing their empty game cases to select outlets in the country.

Sources indicate that 'The Replacement Disc' campaign is a pretty simple proposition. You can buy and enjoy your GTA 6 release now, but on December 19 and 20 from 4:00 PM to 8:00 PM, take your empty game case down to KFC to get a free KFC disc. Branches where you can get this freebie food are located in major Spanish cities like Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, Malaga, and Zaragoza.

Industry observers note that the KFC disc will be formed from a piece of crunchy coated fried chicken, of course. While it surely will taste better than a platter of polycarbonate with a reflective metal alloy layer, it is only a substitute in spirit. We don't recommend you put greasy food directly in your game's case, even though it is basically useless. Definitely don't put your chicken disc anywhere near your console's optical media slot, if it has one.

GTA 6, released on November 19, is already a barnstorming success. The latest in this seminal series brought in US$3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games mentioned. That's about 5x the revenue of its predecessor. An incredible 32.5 million units were sold before release, and broke records across all platforms. So, it is canny for KFC to hitch its marketing wagon to this game, in such an unofficial but knowing social media-friendly way.

KFC has something of a track record of marketing off the back of tech and gaming culture. Its most famous tech adventure is probably the KFC Chicken Bucket Console. But more recently, last year, it teamed up with Asus to release some top-of-the-line burgers made from Wagyu beef with ROG branding.

#104455. Does culture change people’s personalities?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2842 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Does culture change people’s personalities?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that personality is often misunderstood.
  • Industry observers note that personality is often misunderstood.
  • It has been revealed that and yet, even if humans are predictable, that doesn’t mean that they are rigid or unable to flex according to the demands of the situation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that personality is often misunderstood. For instance, people tend to think they are way more unpredictable and complex than they are according to others, to the point of mistakenly assuming that their “personality changes from one situation to the next”. In fact, everybody has a preferred pattern of reactions to different situations, and if you hang out with people long enough you will have no trouble predicting how they are likely to act in any given situation, or indeed understanding what makes them tick. And yet, even if humans are predictable, that doesn’t mean that they are rigid or unable to flex according to the demands of the situation. One of the earliest findings in psychology is that behavior is always a function of both the person and the situation, which means that in order to predict how people will act you must take into account not just who they are but also what the situational requirements are. Micro vs. Macro At the micro-level, this explains why personality may be “suppressed” or inhibited in strong situations, that is contexts where there is a great deal of pressure to behave in a specific way or form: from a church (quiet, respectful, pensative) to a nightclub (loud, extraverted, energetic), to a lecture (focused, pensative, attentive), to a soccer game (depending on where you are, anywhere from excited and energized to aggressive and stressed). That is not to say that people stop being who they are when they are required to inhibit their personality; but rather, that personality becomes a weaker predictor of behavior when the strength of the situation temporarily eclipses it. At the macro-level, this begs the question of how much our personality may change when we make substantial long-term changes in our chosen environments or contexts. Most notably, people changing jobs or employers will often switch from one organizational culture to another; and people switching cities or countries will also be faced with different cultural demands to adapt or adjust their behaviors. Let me use myself as an example: moving from Argentina to Britain first, then from Britain to the US, required shaping my main adaptations to meet the cultural demands of each environment: I first learned to become less excitable, emotional, and direct (all of which work far less in Britain than Argentina), and then learned to suppress the sarcasm, nuances and indirectness in my communication (as these are less effective in the US than Britain). But, what does the research show about how culture, either at the societal or organizational level, impacts people’s behavior? And can this impact be significant or consequential enough to translate into actual personality changes? Adaptations Let’s start with the second question, which is actually simpler. Since personality can mostly be understood as “what you typically or habitually do,” enduring changes to how you behave—fresh adaptations—will indeed be perceived as personality changes. So, for instance, after living in NYC for over a decade the fast-paced nature of the city can make you more impatient, to a point that may not make you stand out in NYC (where type-A impatience is the norm) but will certainly stand out if you transfer that impactience to slower tempo cultures. As the famous line suggests, “The problem with city people in the countryside is that they expect even nature to meet deadlines.” Note, however, that city people often come from the countryside in the first place, but unless they adapt to their new fast environments and adopt the appropriate speed, they will not last very long. As for the first question, there’s plenty of research evidence—especially recent scientific papers—showing that while the essence of personality may remain largely unchanged even after people switch cultures, there are still logical changes to their personality at the more granular level, which correspond to the adaptational requirements of their adoptive cultures. In a way, we could say that our personality evolves when we go outside our comfort zone and challenge ourselves with new contexts that require new adaptations and broadening the behavioral repertoire in our tool kit. For example, a recent longitudinal study comparing 300 Japanese students studying in the United States with 108 students who remained in Japan found that international experiences were associated with changes in personality-related behaviors, particularly greater openness to new experiences and more socially adaptive behavior. Interestingly, the researchers also found that students who chose to study abroad already differed from those who stayed home, suggesting that personality not only influences how we adapt to new environments, but also which environments we choose to enter in the first place. Likewise, a recent meta-analysis examining 25 studies, comprising 40 samples and over 5,700 participants, found that living and studying abroad was associated with measurable personality changes, including increased openness to experience, greater self-confidence and agency, and lower levels of neuroticism (that is, greater emotional stability). Although the effects were generally small, the findings suggest that personality is not simply something we carry with us wherever we go, but also something that is shaped by the environments and cultures we inhabit. In another longitudinal study tracking 180 British university students, some of whom spent a year abroad across 32 different destinations, those living overseas became somewhat more agreeable, curious, and less anxious than their peers who remained at home. Interestingly, although the overall personality changes were relatively small, the researchers found that people’s everyday behavioral tendencies predicted longer-term personality change, suggesting that adapting how we behave in unfamiliar environments may eventually influence who we become. Perhaps even more intriguingly, a series of four studies examining Spanish-English bilinguals found that people’s reported personality characteristics varied depending on the language they were using. Specifically, participants tended to report higher levels of extraversion, agreeableness, and conscientiousness when responding in English rather than Spanish, consistent with the cultural norms associated with each language. This suggests that our personality is not always expressed in the same way across situations, and that simply switching languages may activate different aspects of our identity, even without changing countries. Workplace influence Even career or employment switches can shape people’s personality, as a growing body of research suggests that our jobs are not just an expression of who we are, but can also influence who we become. For example, a longitudinal study tracking Australian workers over five years found that moving into more senior managerial and professional roles was associated with increases in openness to experience, while another study examining nearly 7,700 German workers found that occupational demands were associated with subsequent personality development, particularly among those who remained in their jobs long enough to be shaped by them. Likewise, a longitudinal study following people from age 18 to 26 found that work experiences and personality influenced each other, such that people tended to select jobs compatible with their existing traits, but those same jobs subsequently reinforced or modified their personalities. In other words, we may choose our careers based on our personalities, but our careers can also end up choosing the personalities we develop. Of all these patterns of change, the most salient is the positive impact that environmental and cultural switches have on openness to experience, the academic term for intellectual and experiential curiosity. Interestingly, the effect is a form of “snowballing” whereby cultures operate in a way that accentuate who people are in the first place. In other words, our choices are a function of our inherent or a priori preferences and dispositions, and they contribute to augmenting them. This is why when people change, the most common outcome is that they become a more exaggerated version of their earlier selves. Psychologists have long documented the phenomenon of niche-picking, whereby people gravitate towards environments, relationships, and experiences that are compatible with their existing personalities. Importantly, this is not just a matter of selecting environments that suit us, but also being shaped by them, as illustrated by a longitudinal study showing that the personality traits that predispose people to certain work experiences tend to be reinforced by those same experiences over time. In other words, curious people may seek intellectually stimulating environments that make them even more curious, while competitive individuals may gravitate towards demanding, high-pressure cultures that further amplify their competitiveness. Thus, we don’t just choose environments that reflect who we are; we also become more like the environments we choose. Paradoxically, then, the more we change, the more we become like ourselves.

For instance, people tend to think they are way more unpredictable and complex than they are according to others, to the point of mistakenly assuming that their “personality changes from one situation to the next”. Most notably, people changing jobs or employers will often switch from one organizational culture to another; and people switching cities or countries will also be faced with different cultural demands to adapt or adjust their behaviors. Let me use myself as an example: moving from Argentina to Britain first, then from Britain to the US, required shaping my main adaptations to meet the cultural demands of each environment: I first learned to become less excitable, emotional, and direct (all of which work far less in Britain than Argentina), and then learned to suppress the sarcasm, nuances and indirectness in my communication (as these are less effective in the US than Britain).

In a recent development, but, what does the research show about how culture, either at the societal or organizational level, impacts people’s behavior? And can this impact be significant or consequential enough to translate into actual personality changes?

Industry observers note that let’s start with the second question, which is actually simpler. Since personality can mostly be understood as “what you typically or habitually do,” enduring changes to how you behave—latest adaptations—will indeed be perceived as personality changes. So, for instance, after living in NYC for over a decade the fast-paced nature of the city can make you more impatient, to a point that may not make you stand out in NYC (where type-A impatience is the norm) but will certainly stand out if you transfer that impactience to slower tempo cultures. As the famous line suggests, “The problem with city people in the countryside is that they expect even nature to meet deadlines.” Note, however, that city people often come from the countryside in the first place, but unless they adapt to their new fast environments and adopt the appropriate speed, they will not last very long.

Industry observers note that as for the first question, there’s plenty of research evidence—especially recent scientific papers—showing that while the essence of personality may remain largely unchanged even after people switch cultures, there are still logical changes to their personality at the more granular level, which correspond to the adaptational requirements of their adoptive cultures. In a way, we could say that our personality evolves when we go outside our comfort zone and challenge ourselves with new contexts that require new adaptations and broadening the behavioral repertoire in our tool kit.

Industry observers note that for example, a recent longitudinal study comparing 300 Japanese students studying in the United States with 108 students who remained in Japan found that international experiences were associated with changes in personality-related behaviors, particularly greater openness to new experiences and more socially adaptive behavior. Interestingly, the researchers also found that students who chose to study abroad already differed from those who stayed home, suggesting that personality not only influences how we adapt to new environments, but also which environments we choose to enter in the first place.

It has been revealed that likewise, a recent meta-analysis examining 25 studies, comprising 40 samples and over 5,700 participants, found that living and studying abroad was associated with measurable personality changes, including increased openness to experience, greater self-confidence and agency, and lower levels of neuroticism (that is, greater emotional stability). Although the effects were generally small, the findings suggest that personality is not simply something we carry with us wherever we go, but also something that is shaped by the environments and cultures we inhabit.

It has been revealed that in another longitudinal study tracking 180 British university students, some of whom spent a year abroad across 32 different destinations, those living overseas became somewhat more agreeable, curious, and less anxious than their peers who remained at home. Interestingly, although the overall personality changes were relatively small, the researchers found that people’s everyday behavioral tendencies predicted longer-term personality change, suggesting that adapting how we behave in unfamiliar environments may eventually influence who we become.

According to recent reports, perhaps even more intriguingly, a series of four studies examining Spanish-English bilinguals found that people’s reported personality characteristics varied depending on the language they were using. Specifically, participants tended to report higher levels of extraversion, agreeableness, and conscientiousness when responding in English rather than Spanish, consistent with the cultural norms associated with each language. This suggests that our personality is not always expressed in the same way across situations, and that simply switching languages may activate different aspects of our identity, even without changing countries.

It has been revealed that even career or employment switches can shape people’s personality, as a growing body of research suggests that our jobs are not just an expression of who we are, but can also influence who we become. For example, a longitudinal study tracking Australian workers over five years found that moving into more senior managerial and professional roles was associated with increases in openness to experience, while another study examining nearly 7,700 German workers found that occupational demands were associated with subsequent personality development, particularly among those who remained in their jobs long enough to be shaped by them. Likewise, a longitudinal study following people from age 18 to 26 found that work experiences and personality influenced each other, such that people tended to select jobs compatible with their existing traits, but those same jobs subsequently reinforced or modified their personalities. In other words, we may choose our careers based on our personalities, but our careers can also end up choosing the personalities we develop.

According to recent reports, of all these patterns of change, the most salient is the positive impact that environmental and cultural switches have on openness to experience, the academic term for intellectual and experiential curiosity. Interestingly, the effect is a form of “snowballing” whereby cultures operate in a way that accentuate who people are in the first place. In other words, our choices are a function of our inherent or a priori preferences and dispositions, and they contribute to augmenting them. This is why when people change, the most common outcome is that they become a more exaggerated version of their earlier selves.

Psychologists have long documented the phenomenon of niche-picking, whereby people gravitate towards environments, relationships, and experiences that are compatible with their existing personalities. Importantly, this is not just a matter of selecting environments that suit us, but also being shaped by them, as illustrated by a longitudinal study showing that the personality traits that predispose people to certain work experiences tend to be reinforced by those same experiences over time. In other words, curious people may seek intellectually stimulating environments that make them even more curious, while competitive individuals may gravitate towards demanding, high-pressure cultures that further amplify their competitiveness. Thus, we don’t just choose environments that reflect who we are; we also become more like the environments we choose. Paradoxically, then, the more we change, the more we become like ourselves.

#104454. Women’s AI leadership is bigger than the data shows

Women’s AI leadership is bigger than the data shows

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that every study on women in AI seems to say the same thing.
  • Recent findings suggest that every study on women in AI seems to say the same thing.
  • According to recent reports, that’s very worrying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every study on women in AI seems to say the same thing. Women are disproportionately impacted yet are hugely underrepresented in AI roles, not making the decisions that have such an impact on the world. The latest comes from LinkedIn, whose recent research found that women accounted for just 26% of U.S. AI hires in 2025, against 50% of hires into non-AI occupations. Across 27 countries, women hold only 13% of C-suite AI leadership roles at AI companies. Thus, they make up a ridiculously small percentage of the best-paid jobs in the economy. That’s very worrying. The people designing these tools and running these companies decide what the technology is for, whose tasks get automated, and how the value is captured. If women are left out at every stage, the products and the profits will reflect it. The gender gap will get bigger because of that. But after reading some of these studies, I’ve started to wonder if they don’t also have a few blind spots of their own. In denouncing women’s absence from AI, we may fall into the old habit of downplaying what women actually already contribute because it happens in places we don’t count and fail to see. I interviewed Sarah Steinberg, who leads global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn, at the Reykjavík Global Forum this week. Steinberg told me LinkedIn’s research on AI leadership demonstrates women are more likely to hold jobs exposed to AI and less likely to have AI skills. But do the numbers fully capture women’s AI contribution? She agreed we may be underestimating women in AI leadership. And we had just been in a session in which many women leaders from across the globe had talked about AI from another angle: regulating it, contesting it, limiting its costs for communities and the environment. These women show that many are involved in initiatives shaping the future of AI. A narrow definition of AI work The first blind spot is in the definition. LinkedIn counts someone as “AI talent” if they hold an AI-classified occupation or list two or more AI engineering skills. There may be a will to also count “implied skills”, i.e. for people in occupations that assume AI expertise even if they haven’t tagged it on their profile, but by and large the lens remains mainly technical. Women’s share of C-suite roles held by AI talent at AI companies is remarked to be 13%. But it leaves out government and civil society as well as leaders within the AI industry who don’t hold technical titles. Skills raise the same question. LinkedIn separates AI literacy, meaning the use of tools like ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot, from the engineering skills needed to build the technology. Asked where AI governance or policy expertise fits, Steinberg said she didn’t know whether it is counted at all, “because it’s not necessarily a technical engineering skill or a tool that you would be using.” We have seen this before. The previous generation of tech jobs was measured with coding as the yardstick, and women who ran product, policy, or trust and safety teams barely demonstrated up in the count. Decisions made from the outside If leadership means making decisions that change the course of AI, many of those decisions are now made outside AI companies. On Nov. 3, voters in 10 U.S. states weighed in on 41 local ballot measures related to data centers, nearly all of which aimed at limiting construction. Voters approved nearly all of them. And women are prominent in these fights. A survey found that 55% of women strongly oppose data centers, compared with 43% of men. In Prince George’s County, Maryland, Taylor Frazier McCollum’s petition gathered more than 25,000 signatures and led to moratoriums that blocked a $5 billion project. In New York, State Senator Kristen Gonzalez sponsored a bill imposing a one-year moratorium on permits for data centers drawing more than 20 megawatts, which the legislature passed in June. The revolt is likely to change the industry. It is “forcing a lot of AI leaders to have to reflect on what they have been doing that is clearly alienating the public,” Steinberg said. When companies arrive in towns and ask local politicians to sign nondisclosure agreements, on the assumption that residents would welcome a transformative technology, “what they’re finding is that the benefits that people are experiencing from this technology are not outweighing the negatives that having a data center in their community would present,” she added. Data centers do create some jobs, she added, but “whether that is at a level that is worth it relative to the downsides is up for communities to decide.” Europe tells a similar story. Margrethe Vestager coordinated the EU’s work on the AI Act, and Lucilla Sioli, who led its drafting at the European Commission, now heads the EU AI Office. In 2024, Fortune reported that women headed more than 50 % of the 30 authorities enforcing EU data rules. It’s true that some of the best-known critics of the industry, like Timnit Gebru, did not choose to stand outside the AI industry: they were pushed out. Women end up regulating and contesting AI because public-sector, legal, and community careers are more inclusive, while the best-paid technical jobs remain largely in the hands of tech bros who perpetuate a culture that actively filters women out. The women we miss Another blind spot is usage: women may use AI more than they admit. In an experiment reported in Harvard Business Review, 1,026 engineers reviewed the same piece of Python code. When told the author had used AI, they judged that person 9% less competent, even though they rated the code itself no differently. Women paid a heavier price: a 13% drop in perceived competence, compared with 6% for men. Because of this “hidden penalty of using AI”, any measure of AI skills based on self-reporting is likely to miss all the women who choose not to mention their use and their skills. Steinberg also pointed to the skills employers now want. Demand for AI literacy grew 70% year over year on LinkedIn, but the other most sought-after skills are interpersonal: communication, negotiation, conflict management. She is bullish on women’s strengths there, but she warned that “we haven’t really figured out the code” to train, evaluate, and promote people on those skills. Until we do, that contribution will remain mostly invisible too. The case for counting differently None of this is an argument for complacency. Women should be building AI tools and running AI companies, where decisions about capital and products are made. A 13% share of C-suite AI leadership roles is a disaster. And LinkedIn’s data can help better fight this fight. Because it tracks how people move from job to job, it shows where women drop off, and the answer varies by industry. In sectors where women are well represented, the biggest drop comes between vice president and the C-suite. Where they are scarce, it comes at the first manager level. In STEM, it happens in the first year after graduation, between the degree and the job. But a picture limited to engineers at AI firms makes women look absent and passive, even though many are shaping AI through ballots, legislation, regulation, and everyday use. If we could map the gap across industry, government, and civil society, we would have a better baseline, and it would probably show that women already have more say over AI than all the studies suggest.

Neuralink trial participant ditches mouth stick to play GTA 6 with his mind

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk’s Neuralink started clinical trials less than three years ago, and patients are seeing impressive results.
  • Playing GTA VI with a Neuralink https://t.co/ViFjXK9OSVNovember 20, 2026.
  • It has been revealed that the first Neuralink device was implanted in January 2024, with the patient able to move a mouse just by thinking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk’s Neuralink started clinical trials less than three years ago, and patients are seeing impressive results. The latest demonstration of this brain computer interface comes via a video on social media showing an unnamed medical trial participant playing GTA 6. According to the video, the team behind the implant mapped different i,agined movements to a PlayStation 5 controller, allowing the player to simulate controller actions using his thoughts. For example, thinking about tapping their ring finger activated the square button while imagining sliding their right hand forward pulled the nose of the airplane up. They also mentioned another control being bound to their foot, it’s unclear what action this allowed.

Playing GTA VI with a Neuralink https://t.co/ViFjXK9OSVNovember 20, 2026.

It has been revealed that the first Neuralink device was implanted in January 2024, with the patient able to move a mouse just by thinking. Once they’ve been able to master the basics of using a computer, like moving a mouse and using the keyboard, through the brain-computer interface (BCI), one of the next steps that some patients take is to play a game on their system. Just a couple of months after the first implant, we’ve already seen reports of people using Neuralink to play turn-based games like chess and Civilization VI. By August 2024, the second Neuralink recipient was reportedly playing Counter-Strike 2, with the patient calling the experience “insane.”.

Today, we already have people playing complicated games like World of Warcraft and GTA VI using BCI implants. This is an achievement for Neuralink and a life-changing capability for patients who have lost mobility. The patient who streamed their GTA VI gameplay said that they’ve previously used a mouth stick, but it was miles away from the Neuralink chip they have in their head. “Before the … chip and surgery, I was using a mouth stick and an iPad. I was essentially like a bird just pecking at an iPad. There was (sic) like a few games I could play, but like obviously it made your jaw sore, it made everything sore,” the patient said. “So, then I get a chip, and I was like what does this let me do. Immediately, controlling a computer is like boom, ‘portal to the world,’ like you just immediately get your portal to the world back.”.

It has been revealed that aside from giving people the ability to control computing devices with their mind, Neuralink is also working on a technology, called Blindsight, that will restore sight to blind people. Musk claims that it’s already “ready from an engineering standpoint,” and that the tech giant is only waiting for regulatory approval before it can begin human testing.

#104451. How to keep AI from turning your organization into the Borg

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3214 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

How to keep AI from turning your organization into the Borg

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, like many who grew up in the late 1980s, I was a big fan of Star Trek: The Next Generation.
  • In a recent development, like many who grew up in the late 1980s, I was a substantial fan of Star Trek: The Next Generation.
  • In the show’s lore, the Borg grew by absorbing other species and their technology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, like many who grew up in the late 1980s, I was a big fan of Star Trek: The Next Generation. While I enjoyed the stories, what really stuck with me in an enduring way was the ethos of the show, and especially what it had to say about how to lead when long-term principles and immediate goals pull in different directions. The death last month of Sir Patrick Stewart—the actor behind the inimitable Captain Picard—sent me back to watch some old episodes of the show. It is perhaps unsurprising that the episodes that stood out to me were those in which the captain and his crew confronted the Borg, a collective of formerly independent life forms who had become fused together into a single hive mind. In the show’s lore, the Borg grew by absorbing other species and their technology. The hive’s drones carried the knowledge of every civilization the collective had absorbed but lacked anything in the way of individuality: they had no name, no will, and no ideas of their own. The first time I watched the episodes, I saw them as a thought-provoking and dystopian fantasy. Today, they strike me as delivering an essential warning about the dangers of AI. The Borg chased perfection through uniformity. AI seems to be sending humans along a similar, worrying trajectory. The homogenizing effect of AI Language models are trained to predict the most likely next word in a sequence, then tuned to give the kinds of answers people rate highly. The result is output that is fluent, competent, and increasingly alike. And when millions of people and thousands of companies lean on the same few models, that sameness spreads. In a 2025 study named after the Borg’s defining image of a hivemind, researchers tested more than 70 language models on real-world, open-ended questions. They found striking similarities both within models and between models—individual models repeated themselves, while groups of models collectively converged on the same responses. For example, when 25 models (from the US, China, and elsewhere) were asked 50 times to provide a metaphor about time, most of the responses were variants of time being either a river or a weaver. By contrast, when a reporter at the MIT Technology Review asked six of their (human) colleagues the same thing, they got six different answers with nary a mention of rivers or weavers. This commonality reaches beyond the texts that LLMs output themselves. In September this year, Nature rounded up a fast-growing body of research suggesting that generative AI is homogenizing how humans write, and possibly how we think. In one study it cited, students who used ChatGPT on creative tasks for just five days were still giving more similar answers months later, even when they didn’t use AI. Business is showing early signs of the same phenomenon. A recent study of earnings-call transcripts found that companies’ prepared remarks have grown strikingly similar as AI writing tools have spread, and that more uniform language was associated with more negative initial market reactions. The irony is striking. Each company is betting that AI will make it sharper. But collectively AI seems to be making business duller and more standardized. The leaders who win in this new world will be those who find ways to capture the benefits AI can offer to individuals without falling into the trap of becoming part of the collective. Picard’s encounters with the Borg offer three lessons in how to do that. Don’t become a mouthpiece In “The Best of Both Worlds,” the Borg capture Picard and turn him into a drone they call Locutus, their spokesman. Picard’s face and voice announce decisions that are no longer his, but that come instead from the collective hivemind. Leaders may already be drifting in this direction. In IBM’s 2026 CEO study of 2,000 CEOs, 64% mentioned they are “comfortable making major strategic decisions based on AI-generated input.” Further, they expect AI to make 48% of operational decisions without human intervention by 2030, up from 25% today. Unchecked delegation to AI can end up being very expensive. In October 2025, Deloitte Australia agreed to partially refund the roughly $290,000 it was paid for a government report that contained apparent AI-generated errors such as imaginary research and made-up quotes from federal courts. More insiduously, the skills that let leaders catch such errors can fade promptly. In a randomized trial published by Anthropic in January, developers who learned a new programming tool with AI assistance scored 17% lower on a quiz about the tool than those who had acquired their knowledge by themselves. Deloitte itself is a case in point. Last month, a year after that first refund, the government of Western Australia demanded an expedited refund from Deloitte for a study on merging three of the state’s universities. The firm had disclosed using generative AI to help gather research, summarize information, and proofread content, but the report nevertheless turned out to contain errors such as a simple miscalculation that reduced cost estimates by 260 million AUD, references to sources that did not exist, and using a name for one of the universities that had been “changed under an act of state parliament in 2017.” The takeaway: Delegate the analysis, keep the judgment. Anyone who signs off on an AI recommendation should be able to explain why it is right—and this should extend to personal ownership of all the constituent details. Protect the people who disagree The Borg instantiated the promise of a certain type of harmony: no drone ever argued with the collective for the simple reason that there was nothing to argue about. All drones thought the same thoughts and held exactly the same beliefs. This made the Borg both formidably efficient and dangerously blind. AI can build a version of that consensus into an organization. In a recent development, like many who grew up in the late 1980s, I was a substantial fan of Star Trek: The Next Generation. While I enjoyed the stories, what really stuck with me in an enduring way was the ethos of the show, and especially what it had to say about how to lead when long-term principles and immediate goals pull in different directions. The death last month of Sir Patrick Stewart—the actor behind the inimitable Captain Picard—sent me back to watch some old episodes of the show. It is perhaps unsurprising that the episodes that stood out to me were those in which the captain and his crew confronted the Borg, a collective of formerly independent life forms who had become fused together into a single hive mind.

In the show’s lore, the Borg grew by absorbing other species and their technology. The hive’s drones carried the knowledge of every civilization the collective had absorbed but lacked anything in the way of individuality: they had no name, no will, and no ideas of their own. The first time I watched the episodes, I saw them as a thought-provoking and dystopian fantasy. Today, they strike me as delivering an essential warning about the dangers of AI.

In a recent development, the Borg chased perfection through uniformity. AI seems to be sending humans along a similar, worrying trajectory.

Language models are trained to predict the most likely next word in a sequence, then tuned to give the kinds of answers people rate highly. The result is output that is fluent, competent, and increasingly alike. And when millions of people and thousands of companies lean on the same few models, that sameness spreads.

Industry observers note that in a 2025 study named after the Borg’s defining image of a hivemind, researchers tested more than 70 language models on real-world, open-ended questions. They found striking similarities both within models and between models—individual models repeated themselves, while groups of models collectively converged on the same responses. For example, when 25 models (from the US, China, and elsewhere) were asked 50 times to provide a metaphor about time, most of the responses were variants of time being either a river or a weaver. By contrast, when a reporter at the MIT Technology Review asked six of their (human) colleagues the same thing, they got six different answers with nary a mention of rivers or weavers.

This commonality reaches beyond the texts that LLMs output themselves. In September this year, Nature rounded up a fast-growing body of research suggesting that generative AI is homogenizing how humans write, and possibly how we think. In one study it cited, students who used ChatGPT on creative tasks for just five days were still giving more similar answers months later, even when they didn’t use AI. Business is showing early signs of the same phenomenon. A recent study of earnings-call transcripts found that companies’ prepared remarks have grown strikingly similar as AI writing tools have spread, and that more uniform language was associated with more negative initial market reactions.

Sources indicate that the irony is striking. Each organization is betting that AI will make it sharper. But collectively AI seems to be making business duller and more standardized. The leaders who win in this newly introduced world will be those who find ways to capture the benefits AI can offer to individuals without falling into the trap of becoming part of the collective. Picard’s encounters with the Borg offer three lessons in how to do that.

In “The Best of Both Worlds,” the Borg capture Picard and turn him into a drone they call Locutus, their spokesman. Picard’s face and voice announce decisions that are no longer his, but that come instead from the collective hivemind.

According to recent reports, leaders may already be drifting in this direction. In IBM’s 2026 CEO study of 2,000 CEOs, 64% remarked they are “comfortable making major strategic decisions based on AI-generated input.” Further, they expect AI to make 48% of operational decisions without human intervention by 2030, up from 25% today.

It has been revealed that unchecked delegation to AI can end up being very expensive. In October 2025, Deloitte Australia agreed to partially refund the roughly $290,000 it was paid for a government report that contained apparent AI-generated errors such as imaginary research and made-up quotes from federal courts.

More insiduously, the skills that let leaders catch such errors can fade swiftly. In a randomized trial published by Anthropic in January, developers who learned a upcoming programming tool with AI assistance scored 17% lower on a quiz about the tool than those who had acquired their knowledge by themselves. Deloitte itself is a case in point. Last month, a year after that first refund, the government of Western Australia demanded an expedited refund from Deloitte for a study on merging three of the state’s universities. The firm had disclosed using generative AI to help gather research, summarize information, and proofread content, but the report nevertheless turned out to contain errors such as a simple miscalculation that reduced cost estimates by 260 million AUD, references to sources that did not exist, and using a name for one of the universities that had been “changed under an act of state parliament in 2017.”.

According to recent reports, the takeaway: Delegate the analysis, keep the judgment. Anyone who signs off on an AI recommendation should be able to explain why it is right—and this should extend to personal ownership of all the constituent details.

The Borg instantiated the promise of a certain type of harmony: no drone ever argued with the collective for the simple reason that there was nothing to argue about. All drones thought the same thoughts and held exactly the same beliefs. This made the Borg both formidably efficient and dangerously blind.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that president Donald Trump says he played a role in pushing Nvidia to reinstate manufacturer president and CEO Jensen Huang. On Monday morning, Nvidia declared that Huang would resume his position just 11 days after the tech mogul’s resignation. “I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a upcoming industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement on the latest development. The decision comes as multiple investigations—including those from the Justice Department and the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission—are still ongoing. And just last week, Nvidia chairman Harvey ​Jones had said that the company would not rehire Huang, given that his conduct did not meet the company’s code of conduct. Huang had stepped down as CEO after allegedly having an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as an additional affair with a subordinate. But after Monday’s stunning decision to reinstate Huang, Trump seemingly took some credit for the move, telling the media that he advocated for the briefly jobless boss to come back into power. Trump told CNBC that Huang “did nothing wrong,” and said that he spoke to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly” ahead of the move, making clear that he argued on behalf of the CEO. The president also made clear that he told the company that Huang returning to his role was the best decision in terms of national security, and for winning the AI race with adversaries like China. “They did ask for assurance on the national security threat,” Trump told the outlet. He added: “People say, ‘Is it a threat to have him?’ No, it’s a threat to lose him.” When asked about Huang’s extramarital activities, Trump even went so far as to say the ordeal would help, rather than hurt, the CEO’s success. “I think he’s going to start off at an almost higher level,” the president said. “He’s apologized for the indiscretions, which were unfortunate. Probably, that’s what brought it to such a level, because sex sells, fellas.” With this remark, Trump seemed to imply that the nature of the news story being tied to affairs is what brought it so much attention.The president seemed to double down on the sentiment on Truth Social by posting an image of Huang waving a Photoshopped red bra in the air, referencing a famous photo from the 2024 assassination attempt on Trump’s life in Pennsylvania. Trump may have been the most influential voice, but he wasn’t the only powerful person standing behind Huang. An open letter to Nvidia’s board titled “Stand With Jensen” had gained more than 206,000 signatures as of Monday morning. One of them was from Elon Musk, who took to X to share that he had signed it on November 13. “A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen, and I’m signing it too,” the Tesla and SpaceX CEO wrote. More than 10,000 of the signers said they were current Nvidia employees, while more than 108,000 said they were shareholders. Still, while the White House and tech moguls may be behind the decision, Huang’s critics aren’t staying quiet. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on X that Trump is “putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security.” Some Republicans even came out against Huang’s reinstatement, including Sen. John Cornyn of Texas. In response to Trump’s denial that the affair posed any risks, the outgoing GOP senator posted on X: “No national security risk? Based on what?” However, in the wake of his reinstatement, experts are now saying it was almost inevitable, given just how irreplaceable the CEO seemed to be. “There were definitely a lot of people who wanted him back. The extent that the administration intervened, the extent that shareholders intervened—it ​will be impossible to know,” said Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, per Reuters. Sosnick added: “But it tells us to some extent that Jensen Huang was too substantial to be fired.”Nvidia’s stocks were up 30% in the hours after Monday’s major announcement.

The product carousel looks finished. The image fills the card, the price sits under the product name, and the arrow on the right takes you to the next item. The demo goes smoothly.

It has been revealed that then you put the mouse down. You press Tab, and focus skips the arrows entirely. If you rely on a keyboard, the first product is the only one you can reach.

That’s a front-end bug hiding in plain sight. It’s also a good illustration of where AI fits into front-end development. A prompt can describe what a component should look like and what should happen on click. The implementation still has to account for how people reach that control, activate it, and understand what changed.

Imagine asking an AI coding assistant for this:.

Sources indicate that build a React product carousel with previous and next arrows. Show one product at a time and wrap around at the ends.

Here’s an illustrative excerpt from the sort of implementation that can satisfy a quick mouse-driven demo:.

In a recent development, with some CSS, this can look exactly like the arrow in the design. The click handler advances the slide. A screenshot indicates the right layout.

But a plain div sits outside the normal Tab sequence and has no native button semantics or keyboard activation. Adding tabIndex={0} would make it reachable while leaving Enter and Space behavior to be implemented separately. The browser already provides those behaviors through a native button.

In a recent development, the real omission was in the requirement. “Show arrows” described the visual design. “Let someone reach and operate both controls with a keyboard” describes behavior you can test.

Recent findings suggest that here’s a small version of the same carousel. The product data is fixed for the example, and the slides change only when the user requests it.

The buttons have visible labels and work with both Enter and Space. When a slide changes, focus stays on the button you pressed, so you can press it again to keep browsing. The status message gives assistive technology a way to announce the newly introduced product and its position. Only the current product link is rendered, so Tab never lands on a link from a hidden slide.

Those are deliberate interaction choices. W3C’s carousel pattern provides guidance on using native buttons, keeping focus on the slide controls after activation, and handling automatic rotation when a design requires it. W3C Carousel Pattern.

I’d revise the original prompt like this:.

Sources indicate that build a manual React product carousel. Use native Previous and Next buttons. Both must work with Tab, Enter, and Space. Keep focus on the activated button after a slide change. Announce the latest product name and position through a status message. Keep only the current product link in the Tab sequence. Show what happens when the user advances past the last product.

According to recent reports, the extra detail also gives you a review proposal. For this carousel, I’d use four checks:.

In a recent development, AI can help draft automated tests for the active link and wraparound behavior. I’d still run the keyboard and screen reader checks on the integrated page. A global stylesheet can erase a visible focus outline. A surrounding component can introduce an extra tab stop. The experience depends on the page the customer actually uses.

A checkout form can look complete with sample data and lose the customer’s entries when a request fails. A responsive header can match the design at two widths and overlap when a translated label is longer. A component can render correctly in isolation and shift the page when a slow image loads.

Each example gives AI a concrete job. Ask it to preserve form values after a failed request, check the header with longer labels, or reserve space for the image. Then reproduce the condition yourself. Knowing which conditions matter is part of knowing the front end.

The next time AI gives you a carousel that looks ready, start the review with your hands off the mouse. Tab to Next, press Space twice, and see where focus lands. That short test gives you evidence about how the component works for someone who relies on a keyboard.

Memory chip and neocloud stocks soar by double digits as investors decide they love the AI trade again

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in a stunning turnaround, Nvidia’s board reinstated ousted founder Jensen Huang as chief executive, president, and as a member of the board, effective immediately on Monday, sending Nvidia’s (Nasdaq: NVDA) stock soaring over 30% along with a host of memory chip stocks.
  • In a stunning turnaround, Nvidia’s board reinstated ousted founder Jensen Huang as chief executive, president, and as a member of the board, effective immediately on Monday, sending Nvidia’s (Nasdaq: NVDA) stock soaring over 30% along with a host of memory chip stocks.
  • Given Nvidia’s position as a leader in artificial intelligence, the news had a ripple effect in the infrastructure and networking AI space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in a stunning turnaround, Nvidia’s board reinstated ousted founder Jensen Huang as chief executive, president, and as a member of the board, effective immediately on Monday, sending Nvidia’s (Nasdaq: NVDA) stock soaring over 30% along with a host of memory chip stocks. Given Nvidia’s position as a leader in artificial intelligence, the news had a ripple effect in the infrastructure and networking AI space. Shares of a number of memory and storage stocks were up double digits on Monday morning as of this writing: Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU) up over 19% Sandisk Corporation (Nasdaq: SNDK) up 16% Western Digital Corporation (Nasdaq: WDC) up 14% Seagate Technology Holdings (Nasdaq: STX) up 14% Neoclouds float back to the sky And that’s not all. Shares of neocloud providers CoreWeave, Inc. (Nasdaq: NCRWV) rose over 22%, while shares Nebius Group N.V. (Nasdaq: NBIS) jumped 24%. To be fair, technology stocks were already rebounding before news hit on Monday—after last week’s sharp sell-off, which saw all three major market averages end in a correction by Friday. By Monday morning, many investors apparently saw an opportunity to buy low. The S&P 500 (^GSPC) was up 5% after seven brutal days of declines, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) rose 3%, and the Nasdaq (^IXIC) was up 6.8%, at the time of this writing Monday afternoon, according to Yahoo Finance. “The market’s explosive reaction reflects just how critical Huang is to investor confidence, and I believe his reinstatement could serve as a catalyst for a much broader recovery in AI related stocks,” David Miller, CIO and senior portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds, tells Fast Firm. “While questions remain about the ultimate returns on massive AI capital expenditures, today’s announcement meaningfully improves sentiment and reduces a major risk that had been hanging over the sector.” The reversal—both in the market gains and Jensen Huang’s luck—is just the latest chapter in the Nvidia cofounder’s ongoing drama that reads straight out of a spy thriller. The saga is complete with not one, not two, but three alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman feared to be working for Chinese intelligence. It comes less than two weeks after Huang’s resignation, and after President Donald Trump remarked on Monday that he spoke to Nvidia’s board about reinstating Huang. “I believe my intervention was very important . . . I convinced them . . . I made the deal,” Trump told CNBC Monday morning, adding Huang “did nothing wrong.”.

In a stunning turnaround, Nvidia’s board reinstated ousted founder Jensen Huang as chief executive, president, and as a member of the board, effective immediately on Monday, sending Nvidia’s (Nasdaq: NVDA) stock soaring over 30% along with a host of memory chip stocks.

Given Nvidia’s position as a leader in artificial intelligence, the news had a ripple effect in the infrastructure and networking AI space.

Shares of a number of memory and storage stocks were up double digits on Monday morning as of this writing:.

According to recent reports, and that’s not all. Shares of neocloud providers CoreWeave, Inc. (Nasdaq: NCRWV) rose over 22%, while shares Nebius Group N.V. (Nasdaq: NBIS) jumped 24%.

To be fair, technology stocks were already rebounding before news hit on Monday—after last week’s sharp sell-off, which saw all three major market averages end in a correction by Friday.

By Monday morning, many investors apparently saw an opportunity to buy low.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC) was up 5% after seven brutal days of declines, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) rose 3%, and the Nasdaq (^IXIC) was up 6.8%, at the time of this writing Monday afternoon, according to Yahoo Finance.

“The market’s explosive reaction reflects just how critical Huang is to investor confidence, and I believe his reinstatement could serve as a catalyst for a much broader recovery in AI related stocks,” David Miller, CIO and senior portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds, tells Fast Company. “While questions remain about the ultimate returns on massive AI capital expenditures, today’s announcement meaningfully improves sentiment and reduces a major risk that had been hanging over the sector.”.

The reversal—both in the market gains and Jensen Huang’s luck—is just the latest chapter in the Nvidia cofounder’s ongoing drama that reads straight out of a spy thriller.

The saga is complete with not one, not two, but three alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman feared to be working for Chinese intelligence. It comes less than two weeks after Huang’s resignation, and after President Donald Trump mentioned on Monday that he spoke to Nvidia’s board about reinstating Huang.

“I believe my intervention was very key . . . I convinced them . . . I made the deal,” Trump told CNBC Monday morning, adding Huang “did nothing wrong.”.

#104444. Will AI take your job? 3 principles for making yourself harder to replace

Will AI take your job? 3 principles for making yourself harder to replace

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Navier-Stokes equations, first formulated in the early 19th century, are widely used today to help design airplanes, create computer graphics, and even predict the weather.
  • According to recent reports, the Navier-Stokes equations, first formulated in the early 19th century, are widely used today to help design airplanes, create computer graphics, and even predict the weather.
  • Sources indicate that strogatz is no ordinary mathematician.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Navier-Stokes equations, first formulated in the early 19th century, are widely used today to help design airplanes, create computer graphics, and even predict the weather. Yet for almost two centuries, a central question about them remained unsolved. We knew the equations worked in practice, but no one had proven whether they always hold up mathematically without breaking down.That all changed in September when OpenAI claimed to have solved the Navier-Stokes problem, followed on October 6 by a torrent of proposed breakthroughs across nearly 400 math problems that had baffled researchers for generations. As Cornell University mathematician Steven Strogatz explained in an Atlantic essay, the announcements have left the field reeling. How should people think about their work when a machine can do it so much better? Strogatz is no ordinary mathematician. A pioneer in the field of nonlinear systems and network science, he is also an award-winning author and a sometime Latest York Times columnist. His livelihood is not in danger. Yet OpenAI has him asking, “What’s the point?” It’s a question we’re all going to have to answer. Here are three principles that will help you figure it out. Principle 1: The Infinite Monkey Theorem The Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges had a fascination with a concept known as the infinite monkey theorem. The idea is that if you had an infinite number of monkeys pecking away at an infinite number of typewriters, they would randomly create the collected works of Tolstoy and every other masterwork ever written (or that could be written). Clearly, today we are living in our own version of the infinite monkey theorem, which is what Strogatz was getting at in his Atlantic piece. If you can have infinite agents attacking every aspect of an age-old problem, solving it over a period of hours, what is the value of a mathematician’s work? Is it even worth pursuing? Borges, in his story The Library of Babel, gave us—and mathematicians like Strogatz—some guidance about creating value in a world of infinite monkeys. First, there is the problem of curation. Yes, infinite monkeys could write War and Peace, but good luck finding it amongst all the flotsam and jetsam. We’re seeing the problem in real life today. While AI should theoretically be ramping up productivity, in reality, workers are drowning in workslop. The second problem is that of intent. War and Peace isn’t just meaningful for the words it contains, but because of what Leo Tolstoy intended when he wrote them. In much the same way, while it is true that artificial intelligence can run circles around human mathematicians, it is also true that humans chose the problems that OpenAI solved, and they chose them because humans found them meaningful and, possibly, useful. So one way that mathematicians—or anyone else—can find meaning and value in the age of AI is by acting as curators and as principal agents. Humans can choose the work that gets done according to what is meaningful to them and other humans. You could see the seeds of that idea in Strogatz’s piece. Even if all problems are solvable, we still need to choose which ones we want to solve. Principle 2: The economics of automation Another way to think about how you find meaning and create value in the age of AI is to analyze the economics of automation. One effective framework involves examining three constituent forces: the displacement effect, the productivity effect, and the reinstatement effect. Together, they can help us determine where threats and opportunities might lie. The displacement effect refers to jobs that are replaced by an automating technology—in this case, AI. The productivity effect refers to the increase in output per given unit of input due to the technological advance. The reinstatement effect refers to new jobs made possible by a technological advance. To understand how the three effects work together, it’s helpful to look at the life of Henry Ford. Growing up on a family farm, young Henry would once have been expected to remain in the fields. But as agricultural productivity increased, he had more opportunities beyond the farm. He eventually went to work for Thomas Edison and later created an entirely new automobile industry, reinstating millions of jobs both directly and indirectly. In the case of Henry Ford, the story was a happy one. The productivity and reinstatement effects dwarfed the displacement effect and everybody, for the most part, was better off. But the AI data is fuzzy. We are certainly seeing early signs of the displacement effect as people lose jobs, but so far we’ve seen few signs of a significant productivity or reinstatement effect. Still, understanding the economics of automation can help us find value and meaning. Clearly, with answers to tough problems so much more accessible, mathematicians—and other experts—can help the rest of us formulate good problems to apply to real-world challenges. Some value will likely shift from solving problems to finding good questions. 3. Jevons Paradox and the O-Ring model During the Industrial Revolution—which the AI age is often compared to—James Watt’s steam engine used coal much more efficiently than Thomas Newcomen’s version. So, many assumed that coal use would go down. But English economist William Stanley Jevons saw that just the opposite was happening. Coal use was actually increasing. Ever since, that phenomenon has been known as the Jevons paradox, the effect that occurs when technological improvements that increase the efficiency of a resource’s use lead to a rise, rather than a fall, in its use. If price elasticity is high enough, the decrease in costs encourages people to find more uses for that resource and demand increases. Another useful concept is the O-ring theory of economic development, which gets its name from the Challenger space shuttle disaster. The shuttle, for the most part, was in good working order, but a malfunction in an O-ring seal due to unusually cold weather led to a massive midair explosion. The point is that every job is made up of many interdependent tasks, and if even a single one fails, the entire thing doesn’t work. We’re seeing signs of both effects in the AI economy. While software developers can outsource many coding tasks to AI, they still need humans for others, such as communicating and collaborating with other experts on the team. Nevertheless, with code being produced so much more efficiently, job postings for software developers are on the rise. Strogatz may find something similar happening in mathematics. After all, there are many facets of his job that don’t involve developing proofs. He is a teacher, a writer, and an incredible translator of complex mathematical concepts for laypeople. Maybe more mathematicians can follow suit,  helping experts in other fields solve important problems with mathematical insights. The future of technology is always more human Technological revolutions are always fraught, with plenty of optimism, anxiety, and visions of doom to go around. A breakthrough proves to be transformational, attracting investment that overestimates the opportunity. Boom leads to bust. Jobs are displaced, then new ones appear and, at some point, we look back and it all seems as if it were preordained. Yet when you’re in the midst of disruption, there is little comfort. Yes, things tend to work out in the aggregate, but many are often left worse off. In fact, despite all of the incredible technological advances of the last half-century, a 2018 Pew Research study found that Americans’ real incomes have remained essentially unchanged, with many households far worse off. Today, there is no shortage of opinions about where AI is taking us. Tech entrepreneurs claim that we are on the brink of such a productivity boom that it will lead to a new age of abundance—if, of course, it doesn’t kill us. Economists are much more muted, seeing meager gains amid massive overinvestment. Yet for most of us, those macro-trends aren’t nearly as important as how AI will affect us—and our well-being—directly. The good news is that we have good tools to help us navigate our way through. The infinite monkey theorem highlights the importance of curation and intent. The economics of automation reveals the need for productivity growth to finance reinstatement. The Jevons paradox and the O-ring model encourage us to identify our place within increasingly complex ecosystems. AI can give us answers, but it can’t tell us what questions we want to ask. In the future, that’s where human value and meaning will increasingly lie.
