Not long ago, a synthetic voice was easy to spot: flat, rushed and strangely stressed. Today, the best AI text to speech tools can read a script with natural pacing, switch accents, whisper or laugh on cue, and even speak in a voice cloned from a short recording. That makes them useful far beyond screen readers. Developers use them for product voice prompts, marketers for video voiceovers, teachers for course narration and writers for listening back to their own drafts.

Recent findings suggest that this guide explains how modern text-to-speech works, what to look for when choosing a tool, and compares six options: OpenArt, ElevenLabs, Murf AI, Speechify, WellSaid Labs and Amazon Polly. Each section covers strengths, limits and the best use case. The details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing, and aims, models and prices change often, so confirm current terms before you commit.

Industry observers note that openArt’s AI text to speech tool lives inside a wider creative platform. You open the Audio tab, choose Create voice-over, select a model, paste your script, pick a voice, generate, listen and download. It runs in the browser with nothing to install. According to OpenArt’s page, you can switch between models for each script, including Fish Audio Drama 3, Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo.

The direction system is what makes it practical for storytelling. You add notes in square brackets, such as [whispering], [laughs] or [pause], directly in the script. OpenArt says Fish Audio Drama 3 gives close control over single words and mid-line changes of mood, while Eleven v4 reads the whole script to infer the emotion of each line and keeps the voice steady when you regenerate a line. Preset voices are labeled by accent, gender and age, and you can upload a recording of your own voice to clone it.

Recent findings suggest that because OpenArt also makes video and background music, you can build the voiceover, visuals and soundtrack in one place. It describes a Director mode for planning stories up to five minutes, and the voiceover can also be added in any video editor.

Industry observers note that pricing: New accounts get 40 free credits. Paid plans add monthly credits and watermark-free downloads, and commercial rights apply on eligible paid plans. Check the pricing page for current plans.

Best for: creators who want expressive voiceovers together with AI video and music.

ElevenLabs is one of the best-known names in AI voice. Its text to speech page describes a large voice library, voice design and both instant and professional voice cloning, with the latest model, Eleven v4, positioned as the most expressive. It also lists Eleven v3, Multilingual v2 and a low-latency Flash and Turbo family aimed at real-time use, and it claims support for more than 90 languages and accents, with the exact count varying by model.

Sources indicate that for developers, there is a text to speech API with SDKs, which makes it practical for apps, games, agents and automated pipelines. The free plan includes 10,000 credits a month, and paid looks start with Starter at $6 a month, then Creator at $22 and Pro at $99, according to the vendor page, with introductory offers on the first month.

Sources indicate that pricing: Free plan with 10,000 credits a month. Paid prepares from $6 a month as listed on the vendor page.

Best for: expressive narration, multilingual content and apps that need a voice API.

Murf AI positions itself as a studio for voiceovers. Its page lists more than 200 voices, built with permission and partnership from professional voice actors who earn royalties, and support for 35 or more languages for text to speech, with dubbing in 40 or more. The Studio editor offers pitch, speed and intonation controls and a custom pronunciation library, which helps with brand names and technical terms.

Murf also has an API. Its page describes Falcon 2 for conversational use with time-to-first-audio under 100 milliseconds, priced at $0.01 per minute, and Gen 2 for controllable voiceovers. Gen 2’s “Say it My Way” feature lets you record your own rendition so the model reflects your tone and inflections.

Pricing: Free plan with limits. Paid plan prices are on Murf’s pricing page.

Best for: marketing videos, training and presentations where you want to fine-tune delivery.

Speechify is built around reading aloud. You paste text or upload a PDF, DOCX, TXT or EPUB file, pick a voice, adjust playback speed and listen or download the audio. Its page lists more than 1,000 voices across 60 or more languages, including several regional English accents, and the tool works in the browser and in apps for iOS, Android, Mac and Windows, plus Chrome and Edge extensions.

The use cases lean toward productivity and accessibility: studying, going through emails and documents, language learning and support for people with visual impairments, dyslexia or ADHD. A free account saves your documents and syncs them across devices.

It has been revealed that pricing: You can start free. Paid intends are listed on Speechify’s pricing page.

Best for: students, professionals and anyone who wants to listen to documents and articles.

Sources indicate that wellSaid Labs focuses on professional voiceover for businesses. Every voice is built from recordings of a real voice actor who consented and is paid when the voice is used, and the voices are licensed for commercial use. Its page describes hundreds of voices across languages, accents, tones and styles.

Sources indicate that pronunciation control is a highlight. You can highlight a word to see suggested pronunciations and save your choice to a team library that applies to every project, and set pacing, emphasis and pronunciation line by line. WellSaid also describes a Producer product that connects AI assistants to WellSaid through MCP and its API.

Pricing: Contact sales for a quote based on your voiceover volume.

Best for: corporate training, product marketing, courses and advertising where licensing and consistency matter.

In a recent development, amazon Polly is Amazon Web Services’ text to speech service, and it is aimed squarely at developers. According to AWS, it supports more than 40 languages and language variants with over 100 male and female voices, and it works through APIs in your code. It supports SSML, the W3C standard markup for phrasing, emphasis and intonation, and custom lexicons that fix the pronunciation of acronyms and terms. Output formats include MP3 and OGG.

Recent findings suggest that pricing is usage-based. AWS lists a free tier for new accounts, with usage allowances that depend on the voice engine, so estimate your character volume before you decide. A short example reveals how little code a basic request takes:.

The sample uses the AWS SDK for JavaScript, calls the neural engine and sends SSML so that the pause and emphasis are explicit. Adjust the region, voice and engine to match what your account supports.

In a recent development, pricing: Usage-based with a free tier for new accounts. See the AWS pricing page for current rates.

Best for: apps, IVR systems, notifications and any product that needs automated speech at scale.

Treat this table as a starting point. Features and limits change often, so test two or three tools with the same script.

Modern text-to-speech systems turn written words into audio through several stages.

Recent findings suggest that newer expressive systems go further by reading the whole script to infer emotion and context, and by accepting direction in the text itself, such as a bracketed note that indicates to whisper. That is why a single script can produce very different reads depending on the model and the instructions.

If you use a tool with SSML support, you can make a spoken code or number far clearer:.

The say-as element tells the engine to read the number digit by digit, and the break and emphasis tags shape the rhythm. Supported tags and attributes differ between engines, so check the documentation for yours.

Recent findings suggest that what is the best AI text to speech tool? It depends on the job. OpenArt suits voiceovers with video and music, ElevenLabs suits expressive multilingual audio, Murf AI suits studio-style control, Speechify suits listening, WellSaid Labs suits licensed corporate work and Amazon Polly suits developers.

Is AI text to speech free? Several tools offer free intends or credits, but limits are common. Examples include OpenArt’s free credits for newly introduced accounts, ElevenLabs’ free monthly credits and Murf’s limited free proposal, which has no commercial licence.

Can I use AI voices commercially? Often yes on paid looks, but the rules differ by tool. Always check the current licence before publishing.

Can AI text to speech clone my voice? Some tools support it, including OpenArt and ElevenLabs, usually from a short recording of your own voice. Only clone voices you have permission to use.

In a recent development, what is SSML? Speech Synthesis Markup Language is a W3C standard that lets you control pauses, emphasis, pronunciation and pitch in synthetic speech. Amazon Polly is one service that supports it.

Recent findings suggest that which tool is best for developers? Amazon Polly and ElevenLabs both offer APIs, and Murf describes API options as well. Evaluate latency, languages, pricing and SDK support for your use case.

Industry observers note that how do I make AI voices sound less robotic? Write conversationally, add pauses and emphasis, correct pronunciations and split long scripts into short sections. Choose a model that is designed for expressive reads.

AI text to speech is now good enough for real projects, but the right tool depends on what you are making. OpenArt is a strong first stop for expressive voiceovers alongside video and music, ElevenLabs offers a deep voice library and API, Murf AI and WellSaid Labs suit polished, controlled narration, Speechify turns documents into audio and Amazon Polly fits straight into developer workflows. Test two or three with your own script, check the licence and always listen to the full result before it goes live.

TCL NXTPAPER phones and tablets are all on sale well more than a week ahead of Black Friday, and many models are down to their lowest prices ever.

OLED is wonderful and all, but many of us are feeling the strain from looking at the ultra-bright, extra-vibrant output from these devices. That’s where TCL NXTPAPER technology comes in. NXTPAPER devices were designed to give you all the features and power you need for everyday tasks, all with a screen that’s soft and eye-friendly.

According to recent reports, my favorite budget phone this year just so happens to be the TCL NXTPAPER 70 Pro, which is down to just $259 (21% off) right now for the 128GB model. You can opt for 512GB of storage for just $319 (25% off), too, so folks who need more won’t have to spend an arm and a leg. This sale is even better than the one TCL had just 10 days ago and is the company’s official Black Friday pricing, so while it lasts through November 30, there’s no reason to wait for a better price.

If you’re looking for a tablet, I’ve got two picks that stand out from the rest. The TCL NXTPAPER 11 Plus is down to $199 right now, making it almost 30% off the regular price. This size is perfect for reading books or manga, both of which look superb on the textured, matte NXTPAPER display. I find that this size tablet is sort of the Goldilocks size — big enough to be more useful than a phone, but not too large to be unwieldy.

Folks who are more into taking notes should check out the TCL Note A1 NXTPAPER, which is TCL’s most premium tablet to date and is on sale for $449 right now (25% off). This one has a wildly different UI compared to other TCL products and is intended mostly for note-taking and ideating, although it still runs Android and the Play Store, so you can load anything you want on it. The stylus feels marvelous on the textured, matte NXTPAPER display, and this one packs a newer-generation display than the rest of TCL’s NXTPAPER tablets, too.

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

If you’re shopping for one of the best OLED gaming monitors, the 240 Hz QHD category offers the most choices and the best bang for the buck. But 4K at 240 Hz is creeping downward in price and only represents a small upcharge. It also means that you can go to 32 inches and maintain good pixel density. If you have enough video card horsepower to push frame rates over 180fps, the quality is unmatched.

Sources indicate that samsung slides into the neither-expensive-nor-inexpensive position with its Odyssey G8 G80SH. This 32-inch Quantum Dot OLED runs 240 Hz at 4K resolution with Adaptive-Sync, HDR10, HDR10+, wide gamut color, factory calibration, and high brightness for HDR content. Let’s take a look.

Quantum Dot Organic Light Emitting Diode.

Max Resolution and Refresh Rate.

Recent findings suggest that first, I want to clear up any potential confusion with another recently reviewed Samsung display, the G80HS. That is a 6K resolution dual-refresh mode model that presently costs around $1,600. The G80SH I’m covering here is a 4K screen with a single 240 Hz mode, and it’s currently selling for $900.

The G80SH delivers the best of everything in the premium OLED category. It’s 4K with a Quantum Dot layer that delivers a measured 106% coverage of DCI-P3. That’s about average among the QD-OLEDs I’ve tested, which range from 104 to 108%. The visual difference there is extremely small, not enough to affect a purchase decision. The G80SH also offers excellent out-of-the-box accuracy courtesy of a factory calibration. Though my sample didn’t need any tweaking, it benefited from a few adjustments. And that capability extends to HDR content, where you have full control of color temp, brightness, and luminance tracking.

Speaking of HDR, you get the requisite HDR10 support that all monitors have, plus Samsung’s answer to Dolby Vision, HDR10+. This extension of HDR10 includes dynamic tone mapping where the content matches its luminance curve to whatever display it’s shown on. Since HDR is mastered to a specific peak luminance, usually 1,000 nits but sometimes as high as 10,000, it’s beneficial when the screen can adapt to the incoming metadata to accommodate a lower or higher limit. You’ll see the same fine detail and nuance that the content creator did.

Gaming benefits from the aforementioned 240 Hz refresh rate plus a flawless implementation of Adaptive-Sync. The G80SH works with equal precision on G-Sync and FreeSync platforms, as well as the VRR output from gaming consoles. To help with your aim, there are reticles available in different colors and shapes, with a dynamic mode that keeps them in contrast with the background.

Like every Samsung monitor I’ve experienced, the G80SH delivers high style and solid build quality. The main color is silver, which you can see everywhere except the front, keeping the screen and surrounding bezel all black. There’s a matte anti-glare coating too, effectively eliminating all ambient light reflections. If you have a sunny room, this monitor can handle it without a degradation in image quality. You also get the latest video interfaces, four in total, plus USB and a headphone jack. LED lighting is featured on the back and can be controlled from the OSD.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, so, just to recap before we jump into the tests, this is the Odyssey G8 G80SH, a 4K 240 Hz OLED that sells for $900. If you’re interested in learning more about the 6K model, my review from a few months ago is here.

Samsung still uses crumbly foam to ship its monitors, and my G80SH sample arrived safe and sound. The base, upright, and stand assemble with a captive bolt and a snap-on to create a solid package. To keep the panel thin, the power supply is external. It’s quite large, so consider that when fitting it into your space. The accessory bundle includes right-angle power cables plus one each of DisplayPort, HDMI, and USB-C.

The G80SH’s silver trim is visible from the front in the base and a thin border around the screen that wraps around from the back. The actual bezel is very narrow and flush, so you can’t see it when the power’s off. A small protrusion in the bottom center says Samsung in tiny letters and houses an equally tiny power LED that can’t be seen from the front. Samsung is one of the few manufacturers to offer matte-screened OLEDs, and this implementation is excellent. Even a bright flashlight can’t throw a reflection onto the screen. Sunny office dwellers, this is your monitor.

In the back, it’s all silver all the time with a smooth finish and minimalist styling. There’s a thin ventilation grill on top, a small logo on one side, and hooray, inputs that face backward. You get two HDMI 2.1, a DisplayPort 2.1, USB-C with 98 watts, and two USB-A downstream ports. There are no internal speakers, but there is a 3.5mm headphone jack. On one side of the I/O panel is a joystick, the G80SH’s sole control key. Around the stand’s attachment point is an LED ring with colors and effects available in the OSD. If you remove the stand, a 100mm VESA mount is revealed should you prefer an aftermarket solution. Fasteners are not included.

Industry observers note that that large external power supply keeps the panel thin at just under two inches. The stand is solid and wobble-free and offers 2/25 degrees tilt, 30 degrees swivel, a 90-degree portrait mode and a 4.7-inch height range. Movements are firm and smooth, in keeping with the G80SH’s premium status.

In a recent development, the G80SH’s OSD keeps Samsung’s traditional gaming monitor styling with its control panel appearance. Up top are portholes that deliver information about game-related settings. No refresh rate info, though. It would be nice to have that.

In a recent development, in the Game menu, you get an Adaptive-Sync toggle, aiming points, a black equalizer to enhance shadow detail, and the LED lighting control. The reticles come in two shapes and three colors. Or you can use AI Mode, which changes the color to maintain contrast with the background. You can also position the aiming point somewhere other than the center of the screen. The lighting has multiple effects or can remain a single static color. One miss here is a frame counter. There’s no way to monitor the refresh rate.

Industry observers note that in the Picture menu are all the G80SH’s calibration controls. You get five color temps, all adjustable, and seven gamma presets. The Contrast Enhancer is a field dimming control. True variable brightness is only active in HDR mode. You can choose between static and active tone mapping for HDR, which is handy for HDR10 content because it helps bring out highlights without clipping fine shadow detail.

According to recent reports, you won’t find an sRGB mode among the color space choices, but if you pick Auto, the G80SH will render sRGB for SDR content. This is an approach that I like, and almost no other manufacturers do it that way. If you’d rather see the full gamut for all content, just leave it on Native. Peak Brightness does just what it states for HDR content; it raises the peak output. In my HDR tests, I saw 530 nits from a 25% window pattern.

Remaining menu items include port version control, an off timer, DSC toggle, and USB-C control. You also get two panel care options: logo brightness (dimming, actually) and pixel refresh. You can pause the incoming video signal while this is running if you wish.

The G80SH includes a factory calibration with a report saved in the monitor’s firmware. I found visually perfect color and grayscale tracking, but gamma was a little light. Two clicks of the gamma slider made that much better. I noted that though the default picture mode is called Eco, it is just as bright as the other presets, so that you can use it for all content. In HDR mode, you get Display HDR, which has excellent tone mapping and color accuracy. Suppose you want sRGB; just set Color Space to Auto. Then the G80SH will automatically render sRGB for SDR and the full gamut for HDR, which covers 106% of DCI-P3. If you want full color for SDR, set it to Native. My recommended settings are below.

According to recent reports, the G80SH’s color quality and accuracy make it well suited for duty as a post-production monitor or perhaps an on-site display for location shoots. Only a slight gamma anomaly separates it from perfection. It nails grayscale and gamut tracking, which you can read about on pages four and five. And it’s bright enough for any indoor space. I noted that there was no variable brightness option for SDR, but you can turn on a dynamic contrast option, which equates to field dimming. In HDR mode, dimming occurs at the pixel level, and you can choose between Active and Static tone mapping. The former delivers more punch to HDR10 content.

I also noted the G80SH’s excellent color balance. SDR lets you choose between Native and Auto. Native indicates the full gamut, which covers 106% of DCI-P3 and is very colorful. It will be the likely choice for most consumers. If you prefer sRGB for SDR, set the color space to Auto. Then, it will switch automatically. This is something very few monitors offer. I also noted that the HDR mode allows calibration of grayscale and gamma, another thing I rarely see.

Industry observers note that with the image dialed in, I turned to a few afternoons of gaming where the G80SH provided the addictive quality that all premium OLEDs have. It doesn’t have a frame counter, so I had to use FRAPS to monitor the refresh rate, which stayed around 200fps at the max detail settings in Doom Eternal. This was fast enough to provide blur-free motion and input lag low enough to keep up with my most frenetic movements. You’ll see on the next page that it offers response typical of other 4K 240 Hz OLEDs. That means you’ll be able to aim and shoot with speed and precision. I got extra credit in hoard mode for jump shots where I was able to land grenades on target while flying through the air. Turn and shoot became second nature as I mowed through my opponents.

Detail in close encounters made me stop and admire the picture more than a few times. Tiny highlights like sweat and other bodily fluids popped right out, making the characters look three-dimensional. Other textures like stone and metal looked better thanks to strong reflections. These highlights moved smoothly over objects like the player’s weapon, which further enhanced realism. The G80SH has some of the best-looking HDR I’ve seen of late.

It makes a great workday monitor too, with understated styling that stands out but doesn’t scream for attention. The LED lighting is just a ring in the back with smoothly playing effects or static colors available, or you can shut it off. The stand is rock solid with comfortable and usable ergonomics. The joystick navigates the OSD intuitively and efficiently. I really appreciated the rear-facing ports, which were easy to see and access. You get two USB-A downstream ports, which can accommodate peripherals once you make a connection to the USB-C input, which doubles as a charger with 98 watts of power. There are no internal speakers, but headphones plug into the 3.5mm jack.

Recent findings suggest that takeaway: If Samsung keeps the G80SH’s price below $1,000, it will sell a lot of them. It’s a super versatile display for any form of productivity or entertainment. It’s addictive for gaming, with smooth operation and quick response. The image looks stunning in every respect, whether moving or static. Color accuracy is good enough that calibration isn’t required. It has unique but understated styling and excellent ergonomics with a solid stand and rear-facing ports. Aside from a lack of internal speakers, there is nothing missing here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Google Search homepage is embracing Gemini in a big way, with a upcoming sidebar redesign that puts your chat history just a click away.

Google’s AI ambitions have been anything but subtle in their integration with Search, but Gemini and Search have had some clear separations. But, with its latest update, Google is very much intertwining the two.

Confirmed by Google’s Robby Stein on Twitter/X, Google is now rolling out a desktop homepage revamp that gives Gemini near-top billing.

At first glance, you’ve got the typical blank canvas with a Google logo and Search bar at the center, but the new changes start with Gemini-powered shortcuts underneath for actions such as creating images, analyzing files, and “brainstorming” with Gemini.

These replace the existing “Google Search” button.

In a recent development, beyond that, a new sidebar pulls your Gemini chat history and tasks into the Search homepage as well as including a “New chat” shortcut and everything else you’d find in the Gemini desktop app/site. The AI-heavy adjustment is very perhaps one of the biggest embraces of AI in Search since Google introduced AI Overviews and AI Mode.

Stein explains this change is because users are coming to Search with questions that aren’t “one and done.”.

People are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done – and in testing, this sidebar made a massive difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.

The latest Google Search homepage is now rolling out globally, Stein indicates, though we’re not seeing it live just yet on our devices. Sound off in the comments if you’re seeing the new look and whether or not you like this functionality.

In a recent development, every developer has shipped the other kind of page: a lovingly written article or landing page that peaks on launch day and then quietly rots. Screenshots age, statistics expire, rankings slide. Data-driven pages play the opposite game. Built from a living dataset, they republish themselves daily, grow to thousands of URLs, and answer questions nobody had asked when the site released. This guide breaks down how they work, using a real fan-run stats site as the running example: one public dataset in, more than ten thousand fresh pages out.

Recent findings suggest that static pages lose ground because the web moves and they do not. Facts expire, competitors publish fresher answers, and search engines reward pages whose information matches today. A page that cannot update itself must be rewritten by hand, so most sites update a few pages and abandon the rest.

Freshness is not one rule for the whole web; it depends on the query. Nobody needs a CSS tutorial rewritten weekly, but statistics, prices, availability and anything with a season attached decays on a schedule. Developers misjudge this constantly, treating every page like documentation when half their catalogue is really a perishable good. Serve a three-month-old stat as if it were current and readers learn the most damaging lesson a site can teach: do not trust the numbers here.

It has been revealed that then there is the maintenance maths. A hundred hand-written pages each needing one review a year is a hundred small debts, and the interest compounds as the catalogue grows. The team updates the flagship pages, promises to return for the rest, and quietly never does. Data-driven architecture is really a staffing decision disguised as a technical one: humans design the system once, and the system does the updating forever.

Sources indicate that A data-driven site has three layers: a dataset that refreshes on a schedule, templates that turn records into pages, and URL patterns that map every meaningful combination users might search for. Change the data and every page changes; improve a template and ten thousand pages improve at once.

The running example makes this concrete. A fan-built Overwatch stats tracker republishes Blizzard's public hero data on a daily cycle. From that one feed it generates hero profiles, head-to-head matchup pages and multi-condition tier lists: 10,291 URLs in its sitemap, across six languages, with matchup pages alone accounting for 8,586 of them. Nobody wrote those pages. Somebody designed the system that writes them, which is a very different, and much more scalable, job.

Sources indicate that the example runs on Next.js behind a CDN, but the stack is the least notable layer of the three. The same pipeline feeding WordPress, Astro or a static site generator would look identical from the reader's side of the glass. Choose boring technology you already know, and spend your originality budget on the dataset and the templates, because that is where readers will feel the difference.

Recent findings suggest that generated pages stay useful when every URL must earn its existence with data. Set minimum thresholds before a page is published, give each template unique modules its siblings do not have, and noindex combinations with nothing to say. The line between a resource and spam is not automation; it is emptiness.

Quality gates work best when they are public and mechanical. The example site publishes its tier formula openly: 70% of the score from win rate, 30% from pick rate, and a hard floor that excludes heroes picked in under 0.5% of matches from topping the ranking, because a tiny sample cannot prove anything. That single floor is editorial policy expressed as code. Your version might be a minimum number of data points, a minimum price history, or a minimum review count — the number matters less than the fact that the gate exists and applies to every page equally.

According to recent reports, each template also needs modules its siblings cannot copy. A hero profile carries a seven-day trend and its best and worst matchups; a matchup page carries the head-to-head history; a tier list carries the movement since yesterday. Add a short human layer on top — a methodology page explaining the scoring, changelogs narrating what moved — and the catalogue stops reading as output and starts reading as a publication. Google's scaled-content rules target pages manufactured to manipulate rankings with little value; a page that answers a real query with real, current data is the opposite of that. The honest test for any generated URL is simple: if it vanished tonight, would a searcher lose an answer?

Start embarrassingly small: one dataset, one entity type, one template. A football club's results archive, a property portal's sold prices, your own product catalogue — anything structured and refreshed beats a grand initiative. Prove one template earns traffic, then add combinations, languages and dashboards in that order.

What is programmatic SEO? Programmatic SEO means generating many pages from a structured dataset using templates, instead of writing each page by hand. Done well, each page answers a distinct search with real data. Done badly, it produces thousands of near-identical pages, which is where its reputation suffers.

Is programmatic SEO against Google's rules? No. Google's spam policies target scaled content created mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value for consumers. Pages generated from real data that answer real queries are publishing. The deciding question is whether a page helps its reader, not how it was produced.

How often should the data behind pages refresh? Match the refresh to how fast the underlying facts change. Sports and game statistics justify daily pulls, prices often need hourly checks, and reference data may only move monthly. Refreshing faster than reality changes wastes crawl budget and makes 'updated' stamps meaningless.

Do generated pages need unique written text? They need unique value, which is not the same thing. Identical paragraphs on ten thousand pages add nothing, but unique data, comparisons and trends are content in their own right. Add short human-written context per template, and let the data carry the differences between pages.

It has been revealed that how many pages should a first project launch with? Launch with the smallest set that proves the template: one entity type, a few hundred pages at most. Validate that search engines index them and owners engage before adding combinations and languages. Scaling an unproven template just manufactures tomorrow's cleanup job at industrial size.

The sites quietly winning the long game are not publishing more; they are publishing systems. One honest dataset, one well-built template and strict quality gates will outlast a hundred hand-written pages competing on freshness alone. Try it this week: take one dataset you already own, design a single template with four real modules, and ship fifty pages. Watch what the data does next.

Google introduced 3D emoji on Pixel this year, and has just detailed the minimum specifications required to get them on your Android phone.

Update: Google replied on Reddit to “clear up some confusion” about the Help Center page. The listed storage and RAM requirements refer to the “automatic background download via Google Play services on eligible Android 17 devices that didn’t ship with the 3D font preinstalled.” The support article did not make that distinction.

Noto 3D emoji, with its high-resolution bitmap approach, uses less than 220 MB of storage versus the previous 2D vector font that comes in at around 3 MB.

During installation, Google Play services temporarily needs a bit of extra headroom to copy the file into place before immediately clearing its download cache.

Meanwhile, Google said RAM usage is “minimal & transient” as “Android doesn’t load the 3D emoji font file into RAM.” The support page listed 6 GB as a “cutoff to ensure lower-memory devices stay on the lightweight ~3 MB 2D vector font.”.

Noto 3D emoji goes from vector-based 2D emoji to a high-resolution bitmap font. This results in “high-resolution designs” for emoji “with more texture and dimension to characters and icons.” Google has an FAQ section about why the fresh emoji might look low resolution:.

Vector vs. bitmap rendering: Older Android emoji used 2D vector graphics, which scale infinitely to any size without losing resolution. The 3D emoji are bitmap graphics, which are pre-rendered pixel-based images. When these images are scaled up by an app or zoomed in, the pixels stretch, which can cause a softer or lower-resolution appearance.

The Google support article published this week lists the minimum specs your Android device must have to get 3D emoji:.

Sources indicate that the last two bullet points are rather surprising. In fact, Google even lists instructions for checking how much memory and storage your device has:.

In terms of availability, Google claims a supported device will “automatically download the 3D emoji when it’s on Wi-Fi and charging.”.

At this time, there isn’t a way to force download the emoji.

In a recent development, google unveiled 3D emoji in May, with the fresh design shipping on the Pixel 11 in August. It has since arrived on older Pixel devices.

In terms of OEM availability, Google explicitly says “Samsung devices use a proprietary emoji font and do not receive the 3D font upgrade.” Additionally:.

This is also true for third-party messaging apps, such as WhatsApp, who use their own emoji fonts rather than relying on your device’s system font.

3D printer that promises simultaneous printing from all four heads gets $500,000 in crowdfunding

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Co Print Quadro is an Independent Quad Extrusion (IQEX) bedslinger 3D printer, carrying four fully functional printheads on one gantry.
  • Independent Quad Extrusion, or IQEX, is unlike tool-changer 3D printers.
  • According to recent reports, the Co Print Quadro is a non-enclosed bedslinger, and its design is quite similar to the Bambu Lab A1, albeit much beefier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Co Print Quadro is an Independent Quad Extrusion (IQEX) bedslinger 3D printer, carrying four fully functional printheads on one gantry. The 3D printer accessory tech giant’s first 3D printer aims to bring IQEX technology to the masses at a budget price, with an SRP of only $899. It has already raised over $500,000, crushing its goal of only $9,820.

Independent Quad Extrusion, or IQEX, is unlike tool-changer 3D printers. Instead of one print head swapping assemblies, it has four individual print heads. This allows for increased productivity by printing with all four heads at once, or reducing waste by not going through any purging steps.

According to recent reports, the Co Print Quadro is a non-enclosed bedslinger, and its design is quite similar to the Bambu Lab A1, albeit much beefier. The four print heads line up on one gantry, with space for three extruders on either side so they can get out of the way while either of the extruders on the edges can print. It has a large build volume of 300mm3, while the unit itself takes up a massive 780 x 620 mm footprint (2.5 x 2 feet).

According to recent reports, co print claims the Quadro can switch colors in one second, beating out tool changers that still need to park, grab, and home each tool, possibly with some priming as well. The Quadro’s demonstration video still used a prime tower, but it’s likely optional, meaning it can achieve zero color-change waste. What’s even more impressive is the copy printing technology, allowing multiple or even all print heads to print the same objects at once, potentially increasing productivity fourfold. Of course, it also has its own slicer for added IQEX functions, and it’s based on OrcaSlicer, so we’ll likely see community mods that make it do even crazier things.

It has been revealed that the Co Print Quadro is not without competition, however, as another IQEX printer finished its Kickstarter campaign earlier this year: the LightMake L4, raising $3 million in backing over its $50,000 goal. The L4 is an enclosed Core-XY printer with an even bigger print volume of 354 x 370 x 386mm in a smaller 610 x 620 mm footprint while still able to let each print head reach every corner of the build plate. The L4 has the size and enclosure advantage, but Co Print does blueprint to sell an enclosure for the Quadro as well for more demanding filaments. The L4 has two gantries and can also print four objects at once, but it has a much higher SRP of $2,400 compared to the Quadro’s $899.

The Quadro is Co Print’s first 3D printer, but the company is no stranger to 3D printing, providing multi-color upgrade kits for Creality, Elegoo, and Flashforge printers, including open-source printer brands like Sovol, Voron, and QIDI. While the products are mostly viewed positively, many forums complain about Co Print’s customer service and support. If Co Print wants to sell a whole 3D printer, it should be prepared to deal with issues and take feedback.

Our customary crowdfunder disclaimer applies. Remember that crowdfunding a project is not a guarantee of receiving a finished product. Backing a crowdfunded project is akin to an investment; you believe in the project and want it to succeed. You are not purchasing a retail product.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming leak suggests that Samsung is preparing to copy the iPhone’s Dynamic Island feature in the not-too-distant future, to an extent that not many other Android brands have even done thus far.

Sources indicate that copying the Dynamic Island was briefly like a rite of passage for some Android brands, with many wasting almost no time in delivering their own version of the feature. But, on many of those devices, it’s a surface-level ripoff at best. The feature is primarily limited to music apps and timers, rarely working with any third-party apps in meaningful ways. Android has a built-in feature similar to Apple’s but not in the same styling.

Samsung is now preparing its own version of the Dynamic Island, and it seems this one has a bit more meat on its bones.

SamMobile on Twitter/X posted a video and two still images of what appears to be a Dynamic Island clone coming to Galaxy devices. It’s mentioned as potentially coming to the Galaxy S27 series (so, One UI 9.5) and being called “Moment Effects.” A portion of the software explicitly mentions integration with Google Sports, the leak claims, while it seems Samsung is using Live Notifications here, which already support a number of third-party apps.

The current implementation of live activities showing the "chip" in the top bar is honestly far from good.

It negates one of the major pros of Android over iOS: being able to see notification icons in the top bar.

As when the "chip" of the live activity is active/shown, all notification icons will get hidden, even if there's a ton of space left between the "chip" and the constraint of the front camera area - an implementation that makes no sense whatsoever.

I honestly can't fathom how could Google come out with such poor implementation.

I don't particularly like this one from Samsung, but it surely is 1000000 times better from a UX perspective.

The kicker from a UX perspective is that Samsung’s interpretation allows you to swipe between activities, similar to Apple, but the core premise is similar with the island showing around the selfie camera cutout.

According to recent reports, when this feature might surface does remain unclear, but a One UI 9.5 debut would make plenty of sense. That revision is in beta now and due to launch on the Galaxy S27 series early next year.

In a recent development, what do you think of Samsung’s alleged Dynamic Island clone? Personally, I’m on board as long as it proves useful, and it seems to be on the right track compared to most other copycats.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Ryzen 7 9850X3D needs no introduction. It's the best CPU for gaming, without question, leveraging AMD's latest Zen 5 architecture alongside its 3D V-Cache to accelerate frame rates as much as 30% above the competition. It's down to its lowest price ever in the run-up to Black Friday, dropping to $399 after an instant coupon on Amazon.

Although we see frequent discounts on the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, the newer Ryzen 7 9850X3D has rarely gone on sale. At $399, this is one of the best CPU deals we've seen this Black Friday. In fact, the Ryzen 7 9850X3D and Ryzen 7 9800X3D are the same price right now.

If you're after the ultimate in gaming performance, there's no better option than the Ryzen 7 9850X3D. Thanks to its 93MB of L3 cache, this 8-core/16-thread processor can push out class-leading frame rates in every game out there. With only a 120W TDP, it even stays cooler than the competition, saving you a few extra bucks on that expensive AIO purchase.

Sources indicate that as you can see from our CPU benchmark hierarchy, the Ryzen 7 9850X3D is the fastest gaming processor money can buy. The Ryzen 7 9850X3D is identical to the Ryzen 7 9800X3D outside of a slight boost in clock speed. We found that the base Ryzen 7 9800X3D can reach the same performance level with AMD's Precision Boost Overdrive (PBO), and it usually remains the cheaper of the two CPUs. Right now, however, the two chips are the same price.

Sources indicate that the Ryzen 7 9850X3D remains the gold standard for gaming performance. The closest chip without 3D V-Cache is Intel's Core i9-14900K, which itself only provided 78.2% of the 1080p gaming performance of the 9800X3D. That's despite the fact that the chip often runs below 100W in games, and it has access to only eight cores and 16 threads.

Those eight cores can pose some limitations in heavily threaded apps, particularly compared to the Intel competition. If you're less focused on gaming, a CPU like the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus remains our recommendation. If you just dabble in non-gaming applications, however, the Ryzen 7 9850X3D is a great option.

Intel may have superior core counts, but the Ryzen 7 9850X3D comes with eight full, fat Zen 5 cores, and it can clock up to 5.6 GHz, giving you plenty of grunt for content creation applications alongside games. It slots into existing AM5 motherboards with a 600- or 800-series chipset, though you may need a BIOS enhancement.

According to recent reports, this chip comes with AMD's second-gen 3D V-Cache, which places the extra SRAM under the compute die. This gives the cores direct access to the Integrated Heat Spreader (IHS), meaning the chip can boost as well as its non-X3D counterpart without the SRAM acting as an insulating layer.

The Google Home app is better than Nest alone ever was, mostly

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Nest app is officially dead, but it’s worth taking a step back and remembering that, while there are some rough edges, the Google Home app is a better smart home experience than Nest alone ever could have been.
  • The Nest app has been on life support for years now.
  • Realistically, even long-time Nest users have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nest app is officially dead, but it’s worth taking a step back and remembering that, while there are some rough edges, the Google Home app is a better smart home experience than Nest alone ever could have been.

The Nest app has been on life support for years now. Google has been migrating legacy products into the Home app for a while and the last few puzzle pieces came in Nest Protect support, the death of the earliest Nest Thermostats, and other assorted adjustments.

Realistically, even long-time Nest users have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.

Industry observers note that having been personally, deeply invested in Google’s vision for the smart home over the past decade, I’ll say that the Google Home app we have today is better than the Nest app ever was or ever could be. A huge part of that comes from Google Home’s ability to pull together devices from third-party ecosystems. Being able to control your entire smart home from a single app is how the smart home always should have been, and between Google’s work and the Matter standard, we’re finally able to enjoy that pretty seamlessly for the most part. Automations, Google’s actually-useful AI features, and more only sweeten the deal. I’m also a significant fan of what the Home app has become from a UX perspective. While there are always rough edges and bugs to clean up, the customizable homepage and well-organized sections make for a good – not perfect, but good – experience for the end user.

That mentioned, there is one thing that the Nest app’s limited scope benefitted from, and that’s a focus on making your own product great.

📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Penguin shows off photonic memory box at SC26 that can expand AI accelerator capacity over optical links

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (964 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that penguin Solutions showed off its MemoryAI Photonic Appliance remote memory system at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26), with customer samples scheduled for the second half of 2027.
  • According to recent reports, the MemoryAI Photonic Appliance is designed to accommodate up to 576 GB of HBM3E and 16 TB of DDR5 memory, with overall bandwidth targeting 7.2 TB/s.
  • According to recent reports, the Penguin appliance relies on Marvell's architecture that consists of Photonic Fabric Memory Modules (PFMMs) and Photonic Fabric network interface cards (PF-NICs).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that penguin Solutions showed off its MemoryAI Photonic Appliance remote memory system at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26), with customer samples scheduled for the second half of 2027. The device supports up to 576 GB of HBM3E with an aggregate bandwidth of up to 7.2 TB/s, and connects to systems using optical interconnects via the CXL.mem 3.1 protocol. HBM memory capacity is usually one of the major bottlenecks of contemporary AI accelerators, which is why, when developers face it, they tend to add or upgrade their accelerators. Penguin Solutions' new device aims to solve that, but there are drawbacks.

According to recent reports, the MemoryAI Photonic Appliance is designed to accommodate up to 576 GB of HBM3E and 16 TB of DDR5 memory, with overall bandwidth targeting 7.2 TB/s. The external memory box supports three memory access configurations: HBM Direct Mode, HBM-DDR5 Cached Mode, and DDR5 Direct Mode. The first provides access to external HBM3E, the second combines HBM3E and DDR5 in a tiered memory sub-system with HBM3E acting like a write-through cache for DDR5, while the third provides access to DDR5 without an intermediate HBM cache. Meanwhile, hardware semaphores (HSEMs) enable software-managed memory consistency across multiple host processors (i.e., if more than one host processor accesses the same memory location, software can use semaphores to ensure that only one host processor can modify data).

According to recent reports, the Penguin appliance relies on Marvell's architecture that consists of Photonic Fabric Memory Modules (PFMMs) and Photonic Fabric network interface cards (PF-NICs). The device uses eight PFMM modules; each integrates a memory controller, eight DDR5 DIMM interfaces, 72 GB of HBM3E cache, and a photonic interposer with 16 transmit and 16 receive channels operating at 224 Gbps. This provides approximately 7.2 Tbps of aggregate bidirectional optical bandwidth per module, or 57.6 Tbps (7.2 TB/s) for the entire appliance, equivalent to approximately 3.6 TB/s in each direction.

It has been revealed that marvell offers two ways to connect processors to the external memory pool. The first uses a Photonic Fabric network interface card (PF-NIC) with PCIe 6.0 and CXL 3.1 connectivity, which provides up to 2 Tbps of bandwidth and memory access latency below 350ns, excluding PCIe/CXL overhead. The second relies on a Photonic Fabric chiplet integrated into an XPU, which offers up to 14.4 Tbps of bandwidth and latency below 200ns. Both approaches enable processors to access shared memory over optical links across distances of up to 30 meters. Meanwhile, the chiplet approach requires accelerator designers to install the chiplet, while transparent memory expansion using the PF-NIC requires the host to support its memory mapping at both the hardware and software levels.

Marvell's architecture is designed to enable compatible host systems to access external memory through ordinary load/store memory operations rather than RDMA data transfers, but this requires specific hardware capabilities on the host side. Most modern CPUs support PCIe as well as the CXL.mem protocol for memory expansion. However, the situation is different for AI GPUs.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia's data center GPUs support PCIe, NVLink, and various memory management mechanisms, but they do not support a general-purpose CXL.mem host interface for memory expansion. Similarly, AMD's Instinct accelerators use PCIe and Infinity Fabric for connectivity, but they do not generally support CXL.mem. In theory, accelerators without native CXL.mem support could theoretically access the appliance through a CXL-capable CPU, provided their coherent interconnect supports access to CXL-attached memory. However, this would introduce additional latency, which will extend well beyond the advertised sub-350ns figure (which already excludes PCIe/CXL overhead), which could greatly reduce the actual performance benefits provided by extra capacity.

Industry observers note that as a result, PFMMs and Penguin's MemoryAI Photonic Appliance can extend usable memory capacity only for select host systems without major performance penalties. These could include custom XPUs equipped with Marvell's Photonic Fabric chiplets, CPUs or other PUs that support CXL.mem and PF-NIC with memory mapping mechanism, and potentially future AI accelerators that support CXL.mem or integrate Marvell's Photonic Fabric. Obviously, this means that such systems will get an indisputable advantage over machines based on conventional accelerators from AMD and Nvidia in the form of memory upgrades.

Speaking of advantages, we must note that while an aggregate bi-directional bandwidth target of 7.2 TB/s (3.6 TB/s in both directions) seems formidable (it is only a bit lower than memory bandwidth of B300 SXM that comes at 7.7 TB/s), it is set to be shared between multiple accelerators (eight accelerators in a hypothetical scenario), which will provide limited bandwidth to each one. Although Penguin promises transparent access to external memory without modifications to applications, the appliance will require compatible memory management software (in addition to host hardware), which will treat external memory as another memory tier. While extra memory is always welcome, performance benefits of complex multi-tier memory subsystems depend heavily on workloads and efficient data placement. Consequently, the appliance's practical advantages remain to be demonstrated.

It has been revealed that penguin showcased the appliance this week; however, customer samples are scheduled for the second half of 2027, which likely means that the device and/or underlying hardware, firmware, and software need polishing. That noted, practical performance and economic advantages of Penguin's MemoryAI Photonic Appliance remain to be seen when everything works as intended. In any case, do not expect deployments of such systems before 2028. This begs the question of where Penguin Solutions plans to source HBM3E in volume in 2028, when the industry will have transitioned to HBM4 and will be in the midst of transition to HBM4E.

Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

Which Samsung folding phone is right for you? Galaxy Z Fold 8, Ultra, or Flip 8

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that folding phones are entering a new chapter and, if you’re looking to try one for the first time, you might not know exactly where to start.
  • Samsung has three foldables in its lineup this year, two of which are pretty familiar.
  • Recent findings suggest that each one serves a different need, but they all share similar performance and core specs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that folding phones are entering a new chapter and, if you’re looking to try one for the first time, you might not know exactly where to start. In this guide, we’ll take a look at some of the most important questions to answer when buying a foldable, and dissect how Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Galaxy Z Flip 8 fit the bill to figure out which is the best for you, especially if you’re interested in one this holiday season.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

Samsung has three foldables in its lineup this year, two of which are pretty familiar. The Galaxy Z Flip 8 continues the lineup of clamshell-style foldables, offering a form factor similar to that of a classic flip phone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, meanwhile, is designed to be a normal smartphone on the outside, hiding a tablet within. Finally, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the newly introduced kid on the block, offering a compact outer display that opens up to a media-friendly, wider inner panel.

Recent findings suggest that each one serves a different need, but they all share similar performance and core specs. Here’s a quick rundown of the key details on each device:.

It has been revealed that starting with the displays, the book-style Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra both provide outer displays that are fully usable as standard smartphones, while the inner display is useful for multitasking, media, or just getting more space for reading a website or e-book. Samsung’s top-tier specs deliver performance for everything you’d need, with Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy powering everything from demanding games or media-editing apps to day-to-day use.

With each Samsung foldable, you’re getting a fully capable smartphone, but finding the one that’s best for you is a matter of picking your most vital priorities. Cameras, battery life, content consumption, and size are some of the most important points to consider, so let’s take a look one-by-one.

When it comes to cameras, foldables have a tough time. There’s only so much physical space to fit the camera sensors and, with cameras, having more space generally results in a battery overall camera.

That stated, the best camera on a Samsung foldable is undoubtedly on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra has a 200MP main camera that’s similar to the Galaxy S26 Ultra, while it also packs a 50MP ultrawide and something neither of the others offer, a telephoto lens. The 10MP telephoto shooter captures faraway subjects at 3x optical zoom, meaning you’re not giving up on quality when you zoom in. Two 10MP cameras can be found on the displays, with neither sacrificing quality for an under-display look.

Runner-up here is the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which offers a pair of 50MP cameras for wide and ultrawide shots. You can get 2x optical-quality zoom out of the main sensor to still get a good zoom shot, while the main camera still offers good quality and Samsung’s best camera features including 2x optical-quality zoom and the subject-tracking My FanCam.

According to recent reports, the Galaxy Z Flip 8 may not have the best camera hardware, but what it lacks in hardware it makes up for in flexibility. This is definitely the best form factor of the bunch for using the foldable design as a tripod for capturing clips. All three devices also use their foldable nature to let you capture full-quality selfies using the rear cameras, which always have better quality than the 10MP dedicated front-facing cameras.

Here’s where specs on paper can tell a different story compared to real life.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra may offer the biggest battery of the bunch at 5,000 mAh, but its battery life is on par with the smaller Galaxy Z Fold 8. Both foldables are designed to last you through a full day, though sticking to the outer display only on the Fold 8 Ultra may bring you slightly better battery life overall.

In either case, you’re also getting 45W fast charging over USB-C, granting you speedy recharging if your device happens to get low through the course of a busy day. These are also “Qi2 Ready,” meaning you can use magnetic wireless chargers if you use a compatible magnetic case.

One of the most important things you’ll want to ask yourself when buying a foldable phone is why you want to opt for a foldable in the first place, and each of these devices gives a different answer.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is a productivity powerhouse, delivering more space on its inner display for you to get work done through the web, apps, and more. You can run up to three apps at once on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s display, as well as floating apps, and more.

Recent findings suggest that galaxy Z Fold 8 is great for media consumption. The wider aspect ratio is perfect for watching videos, playing games, reading books, and more, all while still giving you plenty of space for productivity just like the Ultra.

According to recent reports, galaxy Z Flip 8, meanwhile, is all about giving you a more compact device. The outer display lets you quickly reply to messages or keep up with directions, while you can unfold it to do everything you want to on a normal phone. Close it up to more easily stow it away in your pocket or your bag.

If you are moving into a new Galaxy foldable, the good news is that you don’t have to start from scratch. Thanks to Samsung’s Smart Switch app, you can easily transfer supported content including pictures, contacts, messages, and more from an older Galaxy phone, another Android phone, or even an iPhone over to a Galaxy foldable. Apps, messages, photos, and more can all make the move wirelessly, without the need of a cable.

You can get the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra, and Flip 8 from your favorite carriers and retailers, but Best Buy is one of the best places to score a great deal with solid trade-in values and deep discounts around Black Friday and throughout the holiday season.

According to a new report, Samsung’s next “Galaxy Watch 10” won’t be releasing in 2027 with the organization moving to a bi-yearly release schedule for its smartwatches.

ETNews reports that Samsung will not have a latest Galaxy Watch model releasing in 2027, a series that would have likely been called “Galaxy Watch 10.” The reason, the report suggests, is that Samsung is “undertaking a structural overhaul to strengthen profitability” (translated) following two quarters in a row of losses in its mobile division.

Samsung has released a new Galaxy Watch every year since 2018, with 2021’s Galaxy Watch 4 marking the switch to Wear OS.

It has been revealed that the upcoming schedule will apparently see new Galaxy Watch releases every other year, pushing the next release into 2028. The report goes on to mention that Galaxy Watch is part of a “mature phase” of the smartwatch market, and that Galaxy Watch 9 sales “fell short of expectations” likely due in part to its higher price point.

Apparently, Samsung prepares new Galaxy Watch software updates next year as well as “enhancement of healthcare features.” The Galaxy Fit 4 fitness tracker is also expected in 2027, with Dealabs reporting that the tracker will be priced at €79.90 in Europe, a slight price hike over the previous release.

#104303. Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures
